At the federal level, restrict suffrage to people with at least three years of voluntary military service.

For the House of Representatives, eliminate geographic limitations on representation. Allow voters to vote for one candidate from anywhere in the country, and all candidates who receive a certain minimum number of votes are elected for the next two years.

For the Senate, repeal the 17th amendment, so that Senators are appointed to their six-year terms by the state governments that they represent.

At the state and local level, suffrage requirements can be determined by state constitutions. Exception: anyone eligible for federal suffrage automatically qualifies for state/local suffrage.

I don't agree with your proposed changes to the house, the less populous states would become colonies of the more populous states with your system.

And I'd amend the proposed change to federal suffrage to people who have completed two years voluntary military or civic service with or who were honorably discharged from military service for what ever reason.

I think that communications technology has advanced to the point where geographic proximity is no longer the best way to define Congressional constituencies.

The less populated states already have less representation in the House. They are expected to have less representation in the House. The House is supposed to represent the interests of the population directly, while the Senate represents the interests of the States and each State gets an equal voice regardless of population. This is why Senators were originally selected by the State governments. After the 17th Amendment, the States have effectively become mere extensions of the federal government without autonomy.

As far as the service requirement, I would want to be careful in defining what types of service are sufficient. The goal would be to restrict the voting franchise to those who have voluntarily performed a difficult service and put the needs of the nation over their own personal interests.

(Credit for both of these ideas goes to Robert Heinlein. Specifically, he explains them in his books Starship Troopers and The Moon is a Harsh Mistress.)
